setting: Bir kir parkinda gorevlinin ziyaretcilere yeni yuruyus rotalarini ve parkin duzenini anlatmasi
context_line: You will hear a park ranger telling a group of visitors about three new walking routes and about the layout of the park.

turns.speaker: M1
turns.text: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for coming out in the drizzle. I'm one of the rangers here at Stonecrop Country Park. I'll tell you about the three new waymarked routes we opened last week, and then show you where everything is, because the old signs have all come down.

turns.speaker: M1
turns.text: A little background first. This was a working quarry until nineteen sixty-eight, and afterwards it was simply fenced off and forgotten. The council bought it in nineteen ninety-four. What you're standing on is spoil — waste rock tipped here while the quarry was worked — which is why the soil is so thin, and why we get orchids: nothing else grows well enough to crowd them out.

turns.speaker: M1
turns.text: The three routes are colour-coded, and the colours are on the posts rather than on separate signs. The green route is the short one — a mile and a half, flat the whole way and surfaced, so it takes a wheelchair or a pushchair without any trouble. Allow about forty minutes if you're stopping to look.

turns.speaker: M1
turns.text: The blue route is four and a half miles. I know five miles is printed on the older leaflets: we shortened it when the stretch along the river was washed out, so four and a half is right. It's a good two and a half hours, with two fairly steep climbs.

turns.speaker: M1
turns.text: The red route is the long one, seven miles, and it leaves the park for a while and goes up onto the ridge. Boots, not trainers — much of it is on grass and stays wet well into the summer. There's no water on the red route once you leave the visitor centre, so fill something before you set off.

turns.speaker: M1
turns.text: Right — where things are. We're standing at the main entrance, on the Cranmore Road side. As you come in through the main entrance, the visitor centre is immediately on your left, and the car park is opposite it, on the other side of the drive. The toilets are at the back of the visitor centre, and they are the only ones in the park, so I'd use them now rather than later.

turns.speaker: M1
turns.text: Straight ahead of you, where the drive ends, is the information hut. It isn't staffed, but the leaflets live in a box on the side of it and the routes are on a board there as well. Between the information hut and the lake there's a picnic area — half a dozen tables under the trees — and that's the only place we'd rather you ate, because of the ground-nesting birds everywhere else.

turns.speaker: M1
turns.text: From the picnic area, follow the path round the eastern shore and you'll come to the bird hide. It's opposite the small island, which is where the terns nest, with a viewing hatch at child height. Next to the hide, and easy to walk past, is the pond-dipping platform — the low wooden deck sticking out over the shallow end. Nets are free to borrow from the information hut.

turns.speaker: M1
turns.text: Beyond the hide, at the far end of the lake, the ground rises and you'll find the old lime kiln, which is the stone tower with the arch at the bottom of it. You can walk inside as far as the grille. Above the kiln, on the slope facing south, is the wildflower meadow, at its best in June; and at the very top, at the far end of the meadow path, is the viewpoint, a low stone circle with the hills named round it.

turns.speaker: M1
turns.text: The one thing you can't do at present is the boardwalk across the marsh, between the lake and the meadow. Two of the sections have rotted through. I said in the newsletter that it would be open again by the end of May, and I was being optimistic — it will be the middle of June, because the replacement timber is on order and hasn't reached us.

turns.speaker: M1
turns.text: Practical things. The gates are unlocked at eight in the morning and locked at dusk, whenever dusk happens to be, so please don't leave a car in overnight. Parking is two pounds for the day, and there's no charge at all on Wednesdays, which is our quietest day.

turns.speaker: M1
turns.text: Dogs are welcome on the green and the red routes, but they must be on a lead between March and July because of the nesting. The blue route goes through the grazing field, and we ask you to keep dogs out of that one altogether — the cattle are young and they will follow you.

turns.speaker: M1
turns.text: We run a guided walk once a month. It used to be the first Saturday; from this month it's the first Sunday instead, because the survey volunteers needed their Saturdays back. It starts from the information hut at half past ten and lasts about two hours, and you don't need to book unless there are more than six of you.

turns.speaker: M1
turns.text: And we are always short of volunteers. The two jobs I'd most like filled are the scrub-clearing party, which met on Thursdays and has just moved to Tuesdays, and counting the orchids in June, a slow, comfortable job for anybody who can kneel for an hour. There's a sheet on the board by the information hut. Any questions before you set off?

Dort celdirici duzeltme var: mavi rota uzunlugu (bes mil -> dort buçuk mil), tahta yolun acilisi (mayis sonu -> haziran ortasi), rehberli yuruyus gunu (ayin ilk Cumartesi -> ilk Pazar), calilik temizleme gunu (Persembe -> Sali).
